The Program Board

The Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity, under the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, maintains a public program board, its solicitations, program managers, and stated goals published by the agency itself. Its programs describe a single pipeline: uncooperative sensor data turned into a continuous, queryable model of people moving through modeled space.

Preface · the standard of the recordRead 1 min

Preface

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26

This volume separates what the record establishes from what it suggests. Every substantive claim carries its evidentiary status where it appears, in one of four categories.

- Documented. A ratified standard, a funded and named program, an adopted instrument, or a peer-reviewed and replicated result. Cited to its source, carried at full strength.

- Active-research. A capability shown in a laboratory, a simulation, or an animal model, with no fielded system at population scale. The distance to deployment is stated plainly.

- Contested. A claim the scientific record rejects or has yet to settle. Marked as such, the documented substrate beneath it held apart from the assertion built on top.

- Interpretation. A reading that names what the assembled parts amount to. Marked where it is raised, adjudicated where its evidence lives.

Two rules govern the harder cases. Every artifact carries two readings, what it verifiably is and does, and what it serves within the larger architecture. Both readings hold, and the tension between them stays on the record as evidence. Where a new claim presses against a boundary the record already holds, the boundary holds until the evidence moves it.

Published writing enters this report as primary-source evidence of how the defense and intelligence establishment frames these technologies. The report characterizes such writing and cites it. It reproduces none of it. The analysis, the sequence, and the argument are its own.

Introduction · the shape of the inquiryRead 2 min

Introduction

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26

This report treats the human body as an object to be measured, addressed, and operated on. Every technology in it does the same within its own field. Each arrives as a benefit: a sensing advance as better medicine, a networking standard as hospital convenience, a molecular tool as a cure. Named as separate industries, they compose one system, The Apparatus. This volume is its analysis.

The system runs one operation in every field. It measures the body at every scale, and through most barriers. Whatever it measures becomes the default; whatever it misses becomes the gap to close. The fields then converge: ten disciplines, built apart, resolve into one instrument that reads the body and writes to it.

The record is already public, each piece filed under its own innocent heading. A household router, passed through an image model, reconstructs the room it sits in. A standards body has ratified a protocol for networking devices inside the human body and filed it under medical equipment. The United States intelligence community funds the writing and the reading of data stored in DNA. A national research program in Japan commits, in one published list, to freeing the body from its limits and to controlling the weather. Each of these is documented. Each entered the world as the ordinary business of a single field. In sequence, they compose a machine that is plain to see.

The report runs in two sections, in the order the system builds itself. The first covers the integration within the body: the instruments that sense it, the interface that connects to it, the neural and molecular channels that operate on it, and the programs, capital, doctrine, and governance built around them. The second covers the structures that bind those separate integrations into one system: the credential that fixes them to one identity, the agent that acts through them, the money that settles what the agent moves, the compute it runs on, and the emergency that switches it on.

The capabilities are real, funded, and converging. Every part that a single covert in-body system would require is documented, named, and shipped. The one thing the record does not show is the final assembly, the proof that someone has already joined the parts and switched them on inside a population. That proof is the open question of this volume. Everything it would rest on is already here.

Part One · Section 01DocumentedRead 12 min

Perception

The instruments that read the body and its environment across every scale.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 01
1.1

The principle that travels

One idea underwrites all of modern sensing. It predates every machine that now carries it. Impose a known pattern on a signal, acquire an array of measurement as the pattern shifts, reconstruct from the language of the pattern. The detail no individual measurement could resolve. The trick belongs to information, not to any one kind of wave, and that is what lets it move from one carrier to the next unchanged.

Biologists crossed it first, in the microscope. Physicists had long treated the resolving power of a lens as a hard wall, a limit fixed by the wavelength of light. In 2005 Mats Gustafsson walked through that wall without touching the lens. He cast a fine grid of light across a sample too small to resolve, and where the grid crossed the sample's hidden structure it threw off a coarser shimmer, a moiré, the same beat that rises when two window screens slide over one another. The fine structure stays invisible; the coarse shimmer an ordinary lens captures easily. Run the mathematics backward across a few exposures at shifted grid positions, and the structure below the diffraction limit resolves into view. Structured-illumination microscopy broke a barrier the field had treated as permanent. Computation broke it. The glass stayed the same.

Change the carrier from light to sound and the same reconstruction runs unchanged: fire a pulse of laser light into tissue and it comes back as ultrasound, resolving a blood vessel a centimeter beneath the skin. Lihong Wang and Song Hu documented that method, photoacoustic tomography, in 2012, spanning scales from a single organelle to a whole organ by joining optical contrast to ultrasonic depth. Change the carrier once more, to radio scattering through a room, and it still holds. A method proven in a cancer lab does not stay in the cancer lab; the same mathematics that read light now reads radio through a wall.

The instruments that read the body and its environment across every scale.
Part One · Perception
1.2

The room as an instrument

The router on the shelf already sees the room. Every wireless device computes Channel State Information, a running record of how its signal bent and scattered on the way to the receiver, and a body standing in the path writes itself into that record through the reflections it throws. The sensing rides hardware installed for connectivity. That is what keeps it from reading as surveillance. The capability is documented across a decade of peer-reviewed work.

It arrived as a slow escalation, each result reading the living body through a barrier from signal alone. In 2013 Fadel Adib and Dina Katabi, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, tracked a person walking behind a wall with nothing but Wi-Fi-frequency signals and a small antenna array. A year later the same lab placed a body in three dimensions to within ten centimeters through that wall, and taught the system to notice a fall. By 2015 it was lifting breathing and heartbeat off the reflections at several meters' range, contactless, matching the instruments strapped to the subject's chest better than ninety-eight percent of the time.

Then the resolution climbed from motion to anatomy. In 2018 an MIT group trained a neural network on paired radio and camera data until it could draw a fourteen-point human skeleton from the radio alone, through walls and in the dark, with the camera switched off. In 2022 a Carnegie Mellon team pushed the method to its present edge in a paper titled DensePose From WiFi: from the phase and amplitude on three antennas of an ordinary household router, a network rebuilt the full surface of the human body across twenty-four regions, the dense pose a camera had always been required to see. No product ships this yet. The physics is settled, the router is already on the shelf, and the only thing still missing is a trained model.

1.3

The generative turn

A recent advance gave the radio sensor something close to an imagination. In 2025 a group at the Institute of Science Tokyo built a system called LatentCSI that feeds Wi-Fi Channel State Information straight into the latent space of a pretrained image model, Stable Diffusion 3, and lets the model's prior paint a high-resolution, photorealistic picture of the room. The earlier systems detected a body and guessed its pose; this one composes a scene, using the same class of model that renders synthetic art. It needs a model pretrained on the specific room, so it will not conjure a stranger's living room out of a stranger's router. The threshold it crosses is real all the same: pass the ambient radio field through a generative model, and it resolves into an image a person would recognize.

The same principle works through solid ground on hardware that costs a few dollars. At a 2025 sensor conference, researchers from the Harbin Institute of Technology set twelve microcontrollers in a small square and reconstructed objects buried in soil from ordinary Wi-Fi, at image scores approaching the ground truth. The carrier changes, the medium changes, the reconstruction engine does not.

Above the single room, the wireless industry is folding perception into the network itself. Integrated Sensing and Communication uses the same waveform to carry data and to read the space it crosses. It has entered standardization for sixth-generation networks. The industry describes a mobile network that detects, locates, and tracks objects in its coverage, including objects that carry no device, read purely by the way they disturb the field. Deployment is projected for the end of the decade. A parallel line of work builds reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, panels of thousands of tunable elements that reshape how radio moves through a space on command, which turns the room itself into an instrument the sensing layer can shape as well as read. The observation grid assembles inside communication infrastructure, deployed for its own reasons and welcomed on its own terms.

1.4

The body's own chemistry

Motion is the coarse read; chemistry is the fine one. Almost all of it runs on a single material. Graphene, a sheet of carbon one atom thick, is conductive, flexible, biocompatible, and nearly all surface, which makes it an ideal transducer for reading biochemistry through the skin. A 2025 review in Sensors catalogs graphene wearables built for continuous, non-invasive biochemical monitoring, the skin-contact complement to the radio that reads the body from across the room.

The same material carries sensing down to molecular resolution in the terahertz band, the sliver of spectrum between microwave and infrared where molecules announce themselves by how they vibrate. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports pairs graphene with localized surface plasmon resonance to detect blood antigens, reporting absorption above ninety-eight percent and hemoglobin readings across a defined range, aimed at cheap point-of-care testing for anemia. Graphene also builds the antennas and receivers for the short-range terahertz links a body-worn network would need: in 2026 the ICFO institute in Barcelona ran passive graphene sub-terahertz receivers at several gigabits a second over meters. The material that senses the body is the same material that carries its signal, and both advance on one laboratory bench.

1.5

The reconstruction engine

A sensor never measures enough. The gap between a sparse, noisy read and a full picture gets closed by a computation that carries the physics inside it. In 2017 Maziar Raissi, Paris Perdikaris, and George Karniadakis introduced the physics-informed neural network, a model that writes the governing equations of a system directly into its own training target, so the network fits the data and obeys the physics at the same time. The constraint lets it honor known law with almost no labeled data, which is exactly what the ill-posed inverse problems of sensing require: recovering a field, a source, or a whole scene from measurements far too sparse to invert directly.

The method moved into the body fast. A 2025 review for the Annual Review of Biomedical Engineering surveys physics-informed learning across biosolid and biofluid mechanics, medical imaging, and cell signaling, and names it the engine of the physiological digital twin. A 2026 study used it to reconstruct dense three-dimensional cerebrospinal-fluid flow inside a large animal from sparse imaging, holding the reconstruction to the equations of fluid dynamics. One model spans every carrier, optical, acoustic, radio, magnetic, molecular, which makes the fusion of all of them a matter of computation rather than hardware. A scene no longer has to be measured densely to be known; a model that carries the physics fills in what the instruments never sampled.

1.6

The grid that was never installed

The ambition predates the smartphone by a decade. In 1997 Kris Pister, at the University of California, Berkeley, proposed Smart Dust: millimeter-scale motes, each one a microcontroller, a two-way radio, and a sliver of memory, that would scatter into a space, find one another, and blanket it in sensing. DARPAUS Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the defense research arm behind the neural-interface lineage. paid for it. The stated uses ran from nuclear-waste monitoring to building automation to battlefield surveillance. Saturating an environment with self-organizing sensors was a funded objective a quarter-century before a household router learned to picture a room.

That history is the point, because the perception layer arrives by convergence rather than by deployment. Sensing folded into communication through Integrated Sensing and Communication, read off infrastructure already present through Wi-Fi, the room made programmable through tunable surfaces, chemistry lifted through graphene worn on the skin: the capability assembles inside devices and standards installed for other stated reasons, and no dedicated rollout ever marks its completion. The layer that reads the body across every scale accretes through medicine, connectivity, and convenience, one acceptable purpose at a time.

1.7

The unified fabric

Two capabilities this volume has kept apart, the satellite that images the earth and the router that reads a room, are the same system seen at two altitudes. One principle joins them. The wireless industry has written it into a standard. Integrated Sensing and Communication uses one antenna, one slice of spectrum, and one waveform both to carry a signal and to read the space that signal crosses, so a base station talking to a phone measures the bodies between them from the echo of its own transmission. The consequence is structural: every communication node becomes a sensing node, and the sensing grid grows as wide as the communication grid at every altitude. The Third Generation Partnership Project carried the principle from research into specification across its Release 19 track, service requirements in June 2024, an extended channel model in May 2025, a sensing architecture the same year, which puts the capability inside the standard equipment vendors build to rather than in an aftermarket box bolted on later.

The same standard binds the network across altitude through non-terrestrial integration, joining the satellite, aerial, and ground tiers into one addressable fabric. Above the terrestrial tier runs a layered orbital sensing grid already in commercial operation. Electro-optical imaging, close to half of all launches, delivers sub-meter pictures from the constellations of Planet Labs and BlackSky, the latter targeting one-meter resolution at a revisit of ten to fifteen minutes for any point on the surface. Synthetic-aperture radar images through cloud and darkness from Capella Space and ICEYE, with Capella tasking any location within hours and transferring satellite control directly to its customer; Capella launched its eighteenth and nineteenth satellites in January 2026 and its twentieth in March. Radio-frequency payloads from HawkEye 360 detect and geolocate the emitters on the surface, from ship radar to communications. Infrared, the fastest-growing layer, anchors the missile-warning architecture designated a component of the Golden Dome program. The commercial operators hold contracts with the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and the Space Development Agency, and the product is machine-processed: BlackSky's analysis platform fuses optical and radar into activity-based intelligence, monitoring economic and supply-chain movement from orbit. Direct-to-cell service from Starlink and Lynk closes the link between the orbital layer and the handset in the hand.

The join is the operational fact. Non-terrestrial integration keeps a person crossing from open sky to a city street to an interior room inside one fabric, custody passing across tiers on a single network identity. The orbital tier holds the wide, persistent, global frame; the terrestrial tier holds the individual body; and one principle, communication as sensing, runs identically at every altitude between them.

A named network vendor states the thesis in its own terms. Nokia Bell Labs describes sixth-generation networks built to sense their surroundings and the movement of objects within them, a network it calls a sixth sense, alongside a digital twin of reality as a stated use case. Its AI-RAN platform, built with Nvidia and launched for advanced fifth-generation networks in the summer of 2026 with an upgrade path to the sixth, embeds AI-accelerated silicon into the radio itself and claims more than twenty percent and up to twice the spectral efficiency, turning the radio network into an inference layer at the edge. The AI-RAN Alliance carries the standard, the sixth-generation rollout is set to 2030, and the first standards are targeted for late 2028. The network-as-sensor architecture this part documents is, in the vendor's own roadmap, the direction of the industry.

1.8

The continuous scope

At the terrestrial tier the fabric resolves the individual body in fine detail, through walls, from signal alone. The methods appear earlier in this part, the pose reconstructed from Channel State Information and the room composed by a generative model, and they resolve the body's interior as readily as its outline. The same reflections that render a skeleton carry the vital signs: respiration in the band of six to thirty breaths a minute and heart rate from forty to one hundred twenty beats, recovered by filtering the signal a moving chest modulates. A 2025 method named Radio-PPG synthesized the photoplethysmogram, the cardiovascular pulse waveform a fingertip clip produces, from ordinary sixth-generation and Wi-Fi reflection, on the physics that a microwave communication signal penetrates the chest and carries back the rhythm of the heart and the lungs. The authors named its output a digital twin of the cardiovascular signal. The pulse synthesis sits at the research frontier and is marked as such; the pose and vital-sign reconstruction stands on the documented, reproducible record, on hardware as cheap as a mesh of dollar microcontrollers.

The regulators have begun to describe the surface in their own language. In a June 2026 position paper, the conference of Germany's independent data-protection authorities characterized Integrated Sensing and Communication as comparable to an invisible form of video monitoring with significantly broader reach, warned that it collects information from anyone within range including a person carrying no device at all, and noted that an individual would have little practical way to know when a scan is occurring or to refuse it. The statement completes the reading from the governance side. The sensing runs as a standing byproduct of a communication network that never stops transmitting, reads the space in the same signal and the same instant it carries data, and reaches the device-less body without its knowledge. The orbital tier reads the surface from above, the terrestrial tier reads the body in the room, and both run on the communication infrastructure a population asks for, pays for, and carries. Part Two documents the layer that connects to what this one reads.

Part Two · Section 01D · A-RRead 5 min

The Interface

The layer that connects to the body, from ratified spectrum to the molecular channel.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 02
2.1

The body receives an address

The body already has a network address. On 6 February 2012 the board of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers approved IEEE 802.15.6The ratified body-area network standard for devices worn on or in the body (2012, revised 2026)., a document whose stated subject was wireless communication in the vicinity of, or inside, a human body. The specification runs to the level of antenna behavior against living tissue: it defines the media-access and physical layers for a network of sensors worn on the skin or placed beneath it, operating across industrial and nationally approved medical bands, and specifying the limits on how much radiation such a device may deposit in a person. It was developed for healthcare and consumer applications. It named its subject in plain engineering language, without euphemism.

The infrastructure filled in around it on the public record. In a rule that took effect in November 2014, the United States Federal Communications Commission allocated the band from 2360 to 2400 megahertz for Medical Body Area Networks, dividing it between registered health-care facilities and general use and permitting the body-worn devices to communicate directly with one another. The International Organization for Standardization adopted the specification worldwide in 2017. In June 2026 the standards board approved a revision that held the in-body scope and raised the maximum data rate fivefold, to fifty megabits per second, with a clause noting the standard was no longer limited to humans. A ratified protocol in 2012, reserved spectrum in 2014, global adoption in 2017, a faster revision in 2026: the world built a communications standard for the interior of the body, in the open, and filed it under medical devices.

The last engineering obstacle, an antenna that broadcasts from the body without exceeding the exposure limits set for living tissue, has been met with flexible graphene designs that report specific-absorption-rate figures comfortably within the international ceiling. A 2026 graphene-on-textile antenna measured a maximum well under the two-watt-per-kilogram limit at its rated input. The interface is engineered to operate against the body and to stay within the standard that governs radiation into it.

The layer that connects to the body, from ratified spectrum to the molecular channel.
Part Two · The Interface
2.2

The medical bridge

A standard installs the interface. Medicine carries it past the one obstacle that matters, which is refusal. A ratified standard converts a capability into an interoperable, vendor-neutral protocol, and every capability in this domain enters through patient monitoring: the hospital gown that reports vital signs without a tangle of wires, the implant that phones its telemetry to a nursing station. Body-worn and in-body biosensor networks are now a mature engineering field, documented in a 2025 review of chemical and biosensor networks for a connected model of healthcare, reading blood chemistry, cardiac rhythm, and motion and piping the stream upstream.

The mechanism recurs across every domain in this volume. Its name in the defense literature is exact: the dual-use bridge. A capability enters through the channel that manufactures consent, which is medicine. It changes purpose through a change of intent. The hardware stays the same. The monitor that watches a patient and the monitor that watches a person share the same silicon; the difference lies in the reason, and the reason is not written into the device. The un-instrumented body, the body that is a node on no network, becomes the exception once an interoperable in-body layer is ratified, spectrum-backed, and normalized through the clinic years before any question of scale arises.

2.3

The molecular frontier

The interface does not stop at radio. The body's own chemistry is a medium too. In 2015 a team led by the network engineer Ian Akyildiz published, in a mainstream telecommunications journal, a proposal it called the Internet of Bio-Nano Things: an extension of the network down into the body built from engineered biological cells and molecular-scale devices, bridged to the ordinary internet through a translation layer the authors named a bio-cyber interface. The paper set an architecture, and the field has built toward it since.

The communication method at the base of this vision abandons radio for chemistry. Molecular communication encodes information the way a living cell does, in the concentration, the type, and the release timing of molecules that drift across a gap, with a receiver counting the molecules and decoding the message. A comprehensive 2016 survey characterized the field as predominantly theoretical and simulation-based, with tabletop demonstrations and no deployed system inside a body, and that assessment holds: molecular communication and the bio-cyber interface remain active research, marked here as exactly that. A 2021 systematic review catalogued the transduction routes by which a biochemical signal could be converted to an electronic one and back, from bioluminescence to field-effect transistors to redox chemistry, and a 2026 survey proposed a five-layer reference architecture for the field, reporting working channel models and microfluidic testbeds alongside the open problems. The trajectory is documented; the deployment is not.

2.4

The layer that decides what matters

The subtlest change is in what the network decides is worth carrying. Semantic communication, a research direction for sixth-generation networks articulated in a 2023 paper led by Deniz Gündüz, moves the network past the faithful reproduction of bits toward the transmission of meaning, sending the decision-relevant conclusion and withholding the raw stream. A goal-oriented network optimizes sensing, communication, computation, and actuation toward an objective, forwarding only the features that bear on the decision at hand. The efficiency case its proponents make, that transmitting a conclusion exposes less data than a raw feed, describes the same movement from a different angle: the authority to decide what counts as signal migrates into the layer performing the extraction. The network ceases to carry the field and begins to carry its own judgment about the field. Whether the molecular and semantic layers are integrated into a living body at scale is an open question, marked as such, and adjudicated in the final part; the ratified radio standard beneath them stands on the documented record.

Part Three · Section 01D · A-RRead 9 min

The Neural Frontier

Reading and writing the brain, and the fifteen-year program lineage behind it.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 03
3.1

The doctrine of the target

In 2018, from a lecture hall at West Point, James GiordanoGeorgetown and NDU neuroscientist, the recurring byline of the defense neuro-doctrine corpus. told a room of cadets that the brain is the current and future battlespace. The talk was recorded and published under a title that leaves nothing to infer: "The Brain is the Battlefield of the Future." Giordano holds a chair in neurology and biochemistry at Georgetown University Medical Center and has advised the Strategic Multilayer Assessment branch of the Pentagon's Joint Staff and DARPAUS Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the defense research arm behind the neural-interface lineage.'s neuroethics panel. He compressed the operational interface to three verbs, assess, access, affect: to read the brain, to reach it from the single cell to the society, to change it. The doctrine dates its own turn precisely. A 2008 National Academies assessment judged the brain sciences valid for national security but not yet operationally ready; by the middle of the following decade the same body reclassified the field as mature terrain, dual-use and in play. Giordano stated the conclusion to the cadets without qualification, then named the identity beneath it: to affect, he said, is a fashion of saying to target.

The lecture disclosed capabilities that this report carries as attributed disclosure rather than as its own claim. Giordano described nano-scale material engineered for delivery into the body, tuned toward the threshold of detectability and toward the denial of attribution; a consolidation of biological and psychological records into a form that could be retrieved and altered; and a scenario in which a small biological event, amplified through the information environment, produces a population-scale psychological cascade. These are the words of a credentialed authority in a sanctioned venue, and their status as disclosure is documented. Whether the capabilities have been deployed against a population is a separate question, an open one, carried forward and adjudicated at the volume's close rather than asserted here. The interface at the center of the doctrine, the technology that reads neural activity and writes to it, is documented on its own. Its history is a fifteen-year chain of funded programs.

Reading and writing the brain, and the fifteen-year program lineage behind it.
Part Three · The Neural Frontier
3.2

The lineage, from HAND to N3DARPA Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology, a read-write neural interface at ~16 mm³, no surgery.

No single program built the brain-machine interface. A continuous line of them did, each funded on its own justification, and the line is the story the program names conceal. Read in sequence, it records one ambition held constant while the barrier around that ambition falls away, year by year, on the public budget.

The line opens in the mid-2000s with Human Assisted Neural Devices, run by the program manager Geoff Ling and funded, by the estimate of secondary histories, at a hundred and fifty million dollars or more. HAND made brain-controlled prosthetics for wounded service members a fundable defense objective and seeded the cortical-interface competency every program after it drew on. That competency matured into Revolutionizing Prosthetics in 2006, more than a hundred and seven million dollars to the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory by the laboratory's own account, and out of it came the Modular Prosthetic Limb, a seventeen-degree-of-freedom arm under closed-loop cortical control, demonstrated in 2009. It was a wired limb moved by thought.

Then the ambition turned inward, from the limb to the memory. The Restorative Encoding Memory Integration Neural Device, around 2012, built a hippocampal prosthesis under Theodore Berger at the University of Southern California on sixteen point eight million dollars over four years, and its results fed directly into Restoring Active Memory, announced in July 2014: fifteen million to the University of California, Los Angeles, twenty-two and a half million to the University of Pennsylvania, and two and a half million to Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to build the wireless implant, all of it aimed at sensing and restoring human memory. Each step relaxed a constraint the step before it had accepted. The wire gave way to the wireless, the therapy for the wounded became a capability sought for the able, and the read-and-write ambition never moved.

3.3

The nonsurgical threshold

By the middle of the last decade the surgical implant had become the constraint, and DARPA moved to remove it. The Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology program, issued as Broad Agency Announcement HR001118S0029 by the Biological Technologies Office on 23 March 2018, set a phased structure of up to four years and a performance target stated on the agency's own page: the precision to read from and write to sixteen independent channels within a sixteen-cubic-millimeter volume of neural tissue within fifty milliseconds. The figure is the resolution of a surgical implant, specified for a device that opens no skull. On 20 May 2019, under the program manager Al Emondi, DARPA announced six teams: Battelle, Carnegie Mellon University, the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, the Palo Alto Research Center, Rice University, and Teledyne Scientific. The approaches the teams pursued read as a catalog of the carriers documented in Part Four, magnetic, acoustic, optical, and genetic, and the applications DARPA named for the finished interface included the control of drone swarms and cyber-defense systems by thought.

3.4

The interface realized

The brain-computer interface reads and stimulates neural activity. The engineering is documented at full strength, independent of any doctrine. Electrodes, light-sensitive proteins, and emerging graphene and nanomaterial interfaces record from and stimulate the neural substrate, and the Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology program is the noninvasive instance of exactly that read-and-write capability. The interface is the point at which connection and actuation meet on the same tissue: the technology that reaches the brain and the technology that changes it are a single technology, funded across six teams, aimed at a resolution matching a surgical implant.

The integration of this interface with the sensing, storage, and networking layers documented elsewhere in this volume is projection past the record. The report marks it as such. A closed loop joining the brain interface to molecular storage, to molecular communication, and to radio-frequency spatial context, and the claim of noninvasive neural sensing through Wi-Fi or sixth-generation signals, reaches beyond the funded interface and is held below certification. The documented interface and the projected hybrid are kept apart, the first cited to the program record, the second carried as interpretation. The fifteen-year line the reader can now follow year by year is enough on its own: from a wired prosthetic limb in 2006 to a nonsurgical read-and-write interface funded across six teams in 2019, the invasiveness barrier relaxes step by step while the bidirectional ambition holds constant.

3.5

The commercial realization

The program line closed at the funded interface. What follows it is a commercial race, and the race is now the frontier. Investment in brain-computer-interface companies crossed one billion dollars across 2024 and 2025, part of roughly four and eight-tenths billion that entered neurotechnology across some hundred and forty deals in 2025 alone. The capability moved from the agency solicitation to the venture term sheet, and two of the interface's approaches crossed from the laboratory into living humans as products.

SynchronEndovascular brain-computer interface, the Stentrode, backed by In-Q-TelThe Central Intelligence Agency's venture arm: stakes in Palantir, AndurilAutonomous sensing-and-effector company: Lattice, EagleEye, and the IVAS headset program., and Synchron.. carries the nonsurgical ambition of the N3 program into a shipping device. Its Stentrode, a mesh of sixteen electrodes threaded to the brain through a blood vessel with no craniotomy, operates in human participants and enters a 2026 pivotal trial with the Food and Drug Administration aimed at the first premarket approval of an implanted brain-computer interface. Its November 2025 Series D raised two hundred million dollars, and the investors on the round include In-Q-Tel, the venture arm the Central Intelligence Agency founded in 1999, which places the intelligence community directly on the cap table of the commercial read-and-write interface. NeuralinkInvasive brain-computer-interface company in the commercial neural race. raised six hundred and fifty million dollars in June 2025 at a nine-billion-dollar valuation and reports implants of more than a thousand channels in over a dozen human patients. Paradromics carries roughly eighteen million dollars of DARPA funding into a commercial device that drew a breakthrough-device designation in 2023. Blackrock Neurotech, in the Utah-array lineage, took two hundred million dollars from Tether, the stablecoin issuer, a capital line running from programmable money straight into brain-implant hardware. The productization layer the program record stopped short of is now populated, funded, and, for the implanted interfaces, operating in living people.

The non-invasive frontier the N3 program defined has its own venture instance. Merge LabsNon-invasive ultrasound-and-molecular neural interface; seeded by OpenAI's fund., co-founded in January 2026, emerged with a two-hundred-and-fifty-two-million-dollar seed round at roughly eight hundred and fifty million in valuation, the largest check written by the OpenAI Startup Fund, to reach neurons through ultrasound and molecular methods, with no implant. The venture is early, and its own stated rationale names the interface as a translator between the brain's signals and the digital world. That capability sits at the active-research frontier and is marked there. The documented fact is the shape of the field: the fifteen-year program line handed its read-and-write ambition to a commercial sector that now carries it toward consumers, with intelligence capital, defense-program alumni, and a programmable-money issuer all on the funding side.

3.6

The market in the interior

The interface produces a stream, and the stream has become a market. In April 2024 the Neurorights Foundation surveyed thirty consumer neurotechnology companies and found that twenty-nine of the thirty could reach their users' neural data with no meaningful limitation, and that nearly all could pass that data to third parties. The collection instruments arrive as consumer convenience. Meta's electromyographic wristband, revealed in September 2024 to control its augmented-reality glasses, reads neural signals at the wrist as a matter of ordinary operation; Apple patented electroencephalography-sensing earbuds in 2023; a range of headphones and headbands decode attention and sleep and sell at consumer prices. On the invasive side, the implanted interfaces of Synchron, Neuralink, and Paradromics stream continuous data from inside their patients. The endpoint the research names is a brain foundation model, in which the accumulated neural recordings of many users become the training corpus for a multimodal model of brain structure and function, a capability marked here as active research. The interior is rendered as a dataset, and the dataset is rendered as a model.

The legislation is the tell. A society writes its first neural-data privacy laws, Colorado's in April 2024 and California's that September, in the same year the survey finds twenty-nine of thirty companies taking brain data without limit, which means the law arrives to mark the market rather than to precede it. Both statutes extend their protection to the peripheral nervous system, a provision that concedes the point this volume has tracked from the sensing layer forward: the neural signal does not require access to the skull, and the wrist-worn wearable already in the frame reads mental state. The rights side of this thread is adjudicated in Part Nine. The market side runs deeper than any other sensing thread. It feeds the influence layer of Part Twelve directly, because no model of a person runs deeper than a model of the interior. It operates now, through the consumer channel, ahead of the law.

Actuation

Continue
Part Four · Section 01D · A-RRead 5 min

Actuation

Acting on living tissue without contact, and the discipline that polices the claim.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 04
4.1

Light

The most exact demonstration that a nervous system can be given a new input and driven from outside the body restored a fragment of sight to a blind man. In a trial reported in Nature Medicine in 2021, a team led by Jean-Alain Sahel treated a patient with advanced retinitis pigmentosa by injecting into his eye a virus carrying a gene from algae, which built in the surviving cells of his retina a protein that opens when amber light strikes it. Fitted with goggles that translated the visual scene into pulses of amber, the patient located a notebook on a table and touched it, thirty-six times in thirty-nine trials, while cortical recordings confirmed that his brain was seeing. The technique is optogeneticsWriting to neurons with light; established 2005, restored partial vision in a 2021 trial., established in 2005 when Edward Boyden, Karl Deisseroth, and colleagues placed that algal light-switch into mammalian neurons and drove them to fire with millisecond precision under pulses of blue light. Light became a way to write to the nervous system on the timescale at which the nervous system writes to itself. Its limit is depth: light scatters and dies within millimeters of tissue, which confines it to the surface and the eye.

Acting on living tissue without contact, and the discipline that polices the claim.
Part Four · Actuation
4.2

Sound

Sound reaches where light fails. Focused ultrasound, the same physics that images a fetus, can be tuned to a beam that passes through the intact skull and modulates the neurons at its focus, exciting or quieting them without an incision, through a combination of mechanical and thermal effect. Acoustic fields also move matter directly: standing and traveling ultrasound waves exert radiation force that traps, rotates, and transports individual cells without contact, a technique documented under the name acoustic tweezers. The Shapiro laboratory at the California Institute of Technology engineered cells to express gas vesicles, hollow protein structures that scatter ultrasound, making cellular activity visible and steerable by sound, demonstrated in bacteria in 2018 and in mammalian cells in 2019. Engineered acoustic metamaterials, reviewed by Steven Cummer and colleagues in 2016, focus and pattern sound below the diffraction limit, giving the acoustic channel a precision the bare wave lacks. Sound writes to the mid-depth, where light cannot reach.

4.3

The magnetic field and the line the physics draws

A magnetic field passes through bone and tissue as though they were air. It carries the actuation channel into the deep interior. In 2015 Polina Anikeeva's laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology demonstrated wireless magnetothermal deep-brain stimulation: magnetic nanoparticles injected into a target region and driven by an alternating field from outside the skull heat by a few degrees, enough to trip a heat-sensitive channel in the surrounding neurons and make them fire, in a freely moving animal, with no implant and no wire. The mechanism is documented and replicated. It works centimeters deep where light works millimeters.

A more dramatic version of the same claim fails on the physics. Two prominent 2016 papers reported control of animal behavior through a purely genetic magnetic switch, a protein built from the body's iron-storage molecule, ferritin, that would let an ordinary magnetic field flip neurons with no injected particle at all. The physicist Markus Meister examined the claim by first-principles calculation and published the result in eLife the same year: the magnetic energy available to a ferritin particle in such a field sits roughly four orders of magnitude below the thermal energy of the molecules jostling around it, and every proposed mechanism for the effect falls short by six to ten orders of magnitude or more. The switch cannot work, because the physics that would carry it does not exist. The nanoparticle method of Anikeeva's laboratory survives the same arithmetic for a precise reason: an external machine, the alternating field, supplies the energy the lone protein cannot. The distinction is a matter of calculation. A capability real at the nanoparticle scale is impossible at the scale of a bare protein, and the field established the difference on its own instruments.

4.4

The molecular machine

Beneath light, sound, and magnetism runs a fourth actuation layer, one that builds its own machines out of molecules, and its fifteen-year arc reads as a single story of a device learning to do more with less. It began in 2012 with a DNA-origami barrel from Shawn Douglas, Ido Bachelet, and George Church, a container that stays shut until it reads the right combination of molecular signals on a cell's surface, then springs open to release its payload, a logic gate made of genetic material. Two years later, DNA-origami robots ran universal logic, AND, OR, XOR, and a half-adder, inside living cockroaches, the first computation by DNA machines in a live animal. By 2023 the machines worked in three dimensions, folding, positioning, and welding DNA and beginning to self-replicate. A 2025 design carried its own spring-loaded power and chained logic, timing, and cargo release. And in 2026 a bistable DNA switch from the Technical University of Munich toggled between two stable states in milliseconds under an electric pulse, held its state with no continuous energy, and survived roughly a million actuations, the durable, electrically addressable component the field had lacked. Each version did what the one before it could not.

Around that spine, the fleet diversified. Magnetically driven DNA-origami rotors, enzyme-fueled nanomotors, and a nanorobot built from a bacterial membrane vesicle carried the same logic across chemical, magnetic, and biological propulsion, several demonstrated in animal tumor models. A DNA device folded into the shape of a four-fingered hand detected a virus and physically blocked its entry into cells. Capital has begun to follow the science: a company named for the technology raised its first millions in late 2025 to carry DNA-origami delivery toward clinical trials. The molecular machine senses, computes, actuates, and, in the newest work, powers and replicates itself, at a scale no eye and no ordinary microscope resolves. Whether this actuation layer operates at population scale inside the body is the open question of the volume's close; the control science stands on its own as documented, replicated, research-stage biology, advancing through the front door of therapy.

The Substrate

Memory, power, and the quantum ceiling.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 05
5.1

The cell built from parts

In the summer of 2026 a cell assembled from nonliving components did the three things that define life at once: it grew, it copied its genome, and it divided into daughter cells. The work, from Kate Adamala's laboratory at the University of Minnesota and reported first through a preprint, built the cell body from a lipid sac, supplied it with a simplified genome and a commercial pack of thirty-six enzymes, and drew its replication and division machinery from a decade of separate advances. The result sits at the research frontier rather than in the settled record. The report marks it as a preprint whose claims await peer review. Its standing among the field's founders indicates the weight of the milestone: Jack Szostak called it an impressive step, and John Glass called it potentially a watershed for the synthetic-cell field. The substrate this report tracks can now, in prototype, be built from parts.

Memory, power, and the quantum ceiling.
Part Five · The Substrate
5.2

Memory that lives in the genome

Data now lives inside living genomes. In 2018 Weixin Tang and David Liu described a system, CAMERA, that uses the gene-editing machinery of CRISPR to keep a record rather than to cut a gene, writing small permanent changes into a cell's own DNA in proportion to the signals it encounters, so that sequencing the genome later reads back the cell's history of exposures to light, nutrients, drugs, and molecular signals. In 2022 a University of Washington group led by Jay Shendure extended the principle with a molecular recorder that writes symbols into a living genome through sequential editing, demonstrating the recording of thousands of symbols and short text across dozens of editable sites, maintained across twenty cell generations. The genome becomes a rewritable archive of what the cell has seen, the clearest documented instance of a data substrate that lives inside the body rather than beside it.

5.3

The industrialization of molecular storage

The density figures alone rearrange the sense of what a gram of matter can hold. In 2012 George Church's laboratory at Harvard encoded an entire book into synthesized DNA at roughly seven hundred terabytes per gram; a 2017 method approached the theoretical limit and projected a physical density on the order of two hundred petabytes per gram, stable by reasonable extrapolation for thousands of years. The intervening decade turned that proof into an engineering race with a documented funding lineage. United States intelligence money led it. Through the Molecular Information Storage program of the Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity, a consortium announced in 2020 and led by the Georgia Tech Research Institute, with Twist Bioscience, Roswell Biotechnologies, Microsoft, and the University of Washington, drew a contract worth up to twenty-five million dollars and set the targets that still frame the field: an exabyte in a sugar-cube volume, terabyte-per-day writing, and a cost driven toward a dollar per gigabyte. The write infrastructure runs into 2026, where a Harvard silicon chip that synthesizes sixty-four DNA sequences at once names the Office of the Director of National Intelligence among its funders. The intelligence community funds both the writing and the reading of molecular memory.

The commercial edge now promises product. A Twist Bioscience spin-off, Atlas Data Storage, projects a terabyte-scale demonstration and a target of thirteen terabytes in a single drop of water, with cartridges later in the decade. A 2025 academic result encapsulated DNA in a protective mineral shell and claimed a density on the order of hundreds of petabytes per kilometer of tape, with room-temperature shelf life measured in centuries, while honestly reporting that only a hundred and fifty-six kilobytes were actually written, at nearly an hour per cycle: throughput, rather than density, is the present wall. Microsoft's Project Silica pursues the same multi-millennial goal in quartz glass, storing several terabytes in a plate rated for ten thousand years, which shows the drive toward permanent archival memory to be substrate-agnostic. The dense, durable medium is now the object of a funded race with intelligence-community money at its origin.

5.4

Power without a footprint

An implant or a wearable that runs on a battery eventually reveals itself, when the battery dies and someone changes it. The substrate removes that last tell. The human body is a power source: nanogenerators developed by Zhong Lin Wang convert the motion of a footstep or a heartbeat into electricity; flexible harvesters laid on a beating heart, demonstrated by Canan Dagdeviren's group, generate enough current from the organ's own movement to run a pacemaker; skin patches draw power from the gradient between body heat and the air; biofuel cells sip lactate from sweat. A 2025 result integrated a breathable triboelectric fabric, its energy management, a temperature sensor, and a wireless transmitter into a single self-powered garment, a complete body-area sensing node that carries no cord and no charging cycle.

The precise claim matters, because the language can outrun the physics. These harvesters convert energy the body and its environment already spend; the mechanism is transduction of that spent energy, drawing down no biological reserve. What the harvesters change is visibility. A node that draws its power invisibly from its host has shed the last feature that would mark it as a machine.

5.5

The quantum ceiling

Every technology in this volume has a frontier where its promoters point and promise more. The most seductive of those frontiers is quantum. The quantum tools themselves are real and, in places, fielded: algorithms with proven speedups on search and optimization, sensors that read a magnetic field or a radio wave at precision beyond any classical instrument, encryption secured by physical law. The fielded edge is visible in defense. In January 2026 D-Wave Quantum, with AndurilAutonomous sensing-and-effector company: Lattice, EagleEye, and the IVAS headset program. and Davidson Technologies, applied annealing quantum computing to United States air-and-missile-defense planning and reported, in a proof of concept, a tenfold faster time to solution against classical methods and, in a simulated five-hundred-missile attack, the interception of an additional forty-five to sixty missiles. The network layer builds its own quantum substrate alongside: Nokia Bell Labs pairs post-quantum cryptography with quantum key distribution against the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat it dates to a Q-Day around 2030, and pursues entanglement-based quantum networking with repeaters to carry states past the roughly hundred-kilometer fiber limit. These are real, external, machine-scale quantum, and they sit on the far side of a wall from the claim that matters here. The temptation is to extend the line into the body, to imagine quantum-coherent molecular devices woven into living tissue. Here the physics holds. Quantum states are fragile, and a warm, wet, jostling biological medium destroys them almost instantly. In-body quantum computation sits below certification, behind the wall the field calls decoherence.

The promoters' strongest argument against that wall rests on photosynthesis. In 2007 a celebrated experiment appeared to show that a plant harvests light using quantum coherence, in a warm cell at room temperature. If life already did it, the argument ran, an in-body quantum device was merely engineering. For a decade the claim carried enormous weight. A series of careful re-examinations took it apart, culminating in a 2020 consensus review in Science Advances, signed by nineteen of the field's leaders, which reassigned the long-lived signal to ordinary molecular vibration and concluded that coherence does no meaningful work in photosynthesis. The keystone that would have licensed the leap into the body did not hold. The ceiling stands: sensing, connection, actuation, storage, and power are documented; quantum-coherent processing inside living tissue is not.

The Environment

Directed energy, weather modification, and the contested ground held with discipline.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 06
6.1

The documented sky

Directed-energy systems are real and funded. The United States military operates high-energy-laser and high-power-microwave programs, documented in the Congressional Research Service's own reports, and the physics of projecting energy across distance, its limits in fog and turbulence, and the adaptive optics that correct a beam in flight are ordinary engineering. Machines that heat the ionosphere are real and unclassified. The best known, the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program at Gakona, Alaska, fires radio energy into the upper atmosphere from an array of a hundred and eighty antennas driven by a 3.6-megawatt transmitter, so that scientists can study the plasma there; built by the military and operated since 2015 by the University of Alaska Fairbanks, it holds open houses and publishes its research. The operating institution rebuts the folklore point by point: the facility's frequencies pass through the lower atmosphere without heating it, so it cannot steer the weather; it can release no gas or liquid; and mind control lies outside the physics. A documented research heater is not a weather weapon.

Directed energy, weather modification, and the contested ground held with discipline.
Part Six · The Environment
6.2

The scale of the intervention

Weather modification is real, old, and larger in 2026 than casual assumption allows. The numbers come from the government's own accounting. A December 2024 assessment by the Government Accountability Office found nine United States states operating cloud-seeding programs and at least thirty-nine countries seeding clouds between 2020 and 2024, with measured effects ranging from zero to twenty percent additional precipitation and federal oversight the office itself calls minimal. A 2025 dataset published in Scientific Data converted the federal filings into a machine-readable record of eight hundred and thirty-two United States cloud-seeding projects since 2000 and found the activity, after a decline through the 2010s, rebounding sharply in 2024 and 2025. A venture-backed operator, Rainmaker Technology Corporation, runs registered precipitation-enhancement projects across areas of Texas measured in the thousands of square miles. China operates the largest national program on earth, a State Council mandate to cover more than five and a half million square kilometers, an area larger than India, with roughly two billion dollars spent between 2014 and 2021. The United Arab Emirates has added a directed-energy method, a high-power laser system developed at the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi to induce condensation, with a first patent filed in October 2025. The intervention is substantial, accelerating, and thinly governed.

6.3

The solar frontier

The deliberate brightening of the sky to cool the planet has moved from taboo to institutionally funded research. A nonprofit registry tracks fourteen outdoor solar-radiation-modification experiments across stratospheric aerosol injection, marine cloud brightening, and other methods, with names, locations, and dates: most large aerosol trials, including Harvard's SCoPEx, were cancelled under public and governance pressure without releasing material, while smaller marine-brightening and commercial efforts proceed. In March 2026 the Environmental Defense Fund, a mainstream environmental organization, announced funding for nine projects studying the impacts of stratospheric aerosol injection through natural analogues such as volcanoes and wildfire smoke, framed as informing policy rather than endorsing deployment. Peer-reviewed journals now publish staged frameworks for scaling marine cloud brightening from experiment toward deployment and governance typologies for categorizing open-air trials. The field is building the scaffolding of its own transition from experiment to operation, in the open, in the literature.

6.4

The contested ground

The popular version of this territory, the claim that aircraft trails are a covert, ongoing, global aerosol-spraying operation, is not supported by the evidence. In 2016 researchers led by Christine Shearer surveyed seventy-seven of the atmospheric scientists and geochemists best positioned in the world to detect such a program, the people who actually measure what is in the air and the rain. Seventy-six of the seventy-seven reported no evidence of a secret large-scale spraying operation, attributing the trails to ordinary contrail physics and the cited samples to normal environmental chemistry. The covert-global-spraying thesis fails the test set by the experts most able to confirm it.

Both findings hold at once. Weather-modification patents exist; cloud seeding is real and expanding; solar geoengineering is genuinely researched and funded; contrails genuinely spread and warm the climate. A secret worldwide program spraying populations from aircraft is unsupported and rejected by the field. One thread connects this layer to the rest of the volume. As atmospheric sensing folds into the sixth-generation networks and terahertz systems of Part One, the installations that sense the atmosphere acquire, in principle, the capacity to act on it, the same collapse of the boundary between reading and writing seen at the neural and molecular scales. Whether that principle has become a covert operation at scale is undocumented. The report logs it as an open question and leaves it there.

6.5

The sovereign convergence

The solar frontier of Section 6.3 carries architects and funders the aggregate account leaves out, and naming them draws the line from private philanthropy to sovereign commitment. Harvard's SCoPEx, the stratospheric-aerosol experiment cancelled in 2024, was led by David Keith, the central figure of solar-radiation research, since moved to the University of Chicago, with Frank Keutsch as its principal investigator. The near-exclusive funding for the field before governments entered came from private philanthropy: the Simons Foundation committed fifty million dollars over five years, and the Quadrature Climate Fund backed the same work, the money that carried marine cloud brightening and stratospheric-aerosol research from taboo to fundable science. At the unregulated edge, a venture-backed operator, Make Sunsets, releases stratospheric-aerosol and marine-brightening material commercially, and an advocacy organization, SilverLining, builds the policy scaffolding for the field's passage from experiment toward governance.

The sovereign instance gathers the whole convergence under one roof. The United Kingdom's Advanced Research and Invention Agency, created by Act of Parliament in 2022, operational in January 2023, funded at roughly eight hundred million pounds over five years and exempt from freedom-of-information requests, was modeled on DARPAUS Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the defense research arm behind the neural-interface lineage. and built to place large bets on high-risk technology. Its fifty-six-point-eight-million-pound program, titled for the active cooling of the earth, funded twenty-one projects at forty-five million pounds in May 2025, five of them controlled outdoor experiments, the largest single government commitment to solar-radiation modification on record; its director is an electrochemist with no climate-science background who conceived the program. The same agency funds neurotechnology, synthetic biology, and artificial intelligence from the same portfolio. ARIA is the architecture this volume assembles from ten separate fields, gathered inside one funded agency in a second sovereign state, which a program board naming only the United States and Japan would otherwise leave off the map. Part Seven documents that board and the capital that carries it.

The Program Board

Part Seven · Section 01DocumentedRead 9 min

The Program Board

The state and intelligence layer, named and funded.

Field Report · Vol.00108.07.26Section 01 · Part 07
7.1

The constellation

The Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity, under the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, maintains a public program board, its solicitations, program managers, performers, and stated goals published by the agency itself. Its programs describe a single pipeline: uncooperative sensor data turned into a continuous, queryable model of people moving through modeled space.

The pipeline resolves people from data no one collected with consent. BRIARIARPA program for biometric recognition at range and altitude: gait, shape, and face at 300 m and beyond., the Biometric Recognition and Identification at Altitude and Range program, identifies a whole body by fusing gait, shape, and face at ranges beyond three hundred meters and from elevated and aerial platforms, where face recognition alone fails. SMART ePANTS, the Smart Electrically Powered and Networked Textile Systems program, builds functional clothing with integrated audio, video, and geolocation sensors that retains the feel of ordinary fabric. Video LINCS re-identifies the same person or vehicle across unrelated cameras with no prior knowledge of the sensors and drops the result into a common geo-reference frame; LocUS geolocates a video from its sound and image when the metadata is stripped; WRIVA reconstructs a photorealistic, navigable three-dimensional model of a place from scattered imagery; and COSMIC fuses satellite, drone, and ground-camera feeds into a persistent, AI-queryable model of a location. MOVES reads physiological and health state off ordinary video of a clothed person, at a stated long-term objective of assessing the health metrics of individuals and populations from open sources.

The reasoning layer then makes the stream legible. HAYSTAC, the Hidden Activity Signal and Trajectory Anomaly Characterization program, builds models of normal human movement across times, locations, and people, so that anomalous activity surfaces automatically, with a stated target of catching eighty percent of anomalous activity while keeping generated normal activity only ten percent detectable. DECIPHER decodes the coded and evolving language wrapped around those movements. ARTS, the Anonymous Real-Time Speech program, alters a person's speech in real time so it cannot be attributed, and its existence is itself informative: a funded program to defeat real-time voiceprint identification establishes that real-time voiceprint identification is an operational capability treated as pervasive. Underneath sits a compute program, AGILE, built by the agency's own description for predictive rather than forensic analysis. Eight of these programs carry a direct human-tracking, biometric, movement-modeling, or communications-surveillance function, and the design intent the agency states is anticipatory: model the normal in order to flag the deviation before the event.

The state and intelligence layer, named and funded.
Part Seven · The Program Board
7.2

The molecular archive

The most consequential single finding of the program board is that the intelligence community is the documented spine of DNA data storage, through one coordinated effort. The Molecular Information Storage program set the field's still-current targets, and its SMASH consortium, announced in January 2020, distributed the work: the Georgia Tech Research Institute as prime on a contract worth up to twenty-five million dollars, Twist Bioscience on synthesis at up to nine million in fees plus five and a half million for chip design, Roswell Biotechnologies on a molecular-electronic reader targeting ten terabytes per day, and Microsoft and the University of Washington on architecture and coding. The lineage carries forward: the 2026 Harvard semiconductor DNA-writing chip names the same intelligence office among its funders. A state that funds both the writing and the reading of data stored in molecules stands at the archival layer of the whole architecture.

7.3

The national commitment

Where the American programs document the intelligence layer, Japan's MoonshotJapan's JST Moonshot program: Goals 1 and 8 name cybernetic avatars and weather control. program documents state intent in the plainest single artifact in this volume: one national program that commits, in a published goal list, to instrumenting the body and controlling the weather in the same breath. Established in 2020 by the Japan Science and Technology Agency under the Cabinet Office, with targets set to 2050, the program enumerates ten goals, and two of them land on this report's territory.

Goal 1 pursues freedom from the limitations of body, brain, space, and time. Its central instrument is the Cybernetic Avatar, specified in three classes: a socio-avatar that releases a person from physical and spatial constraint, a brain-machine-interface avatar controlled by decoded intention, and an in-body avatar of minimally invasive internal devices for enhancement and health monitoring. The framing is human liberation; the architecture beneath it reads the brain and the body and operates remote effectors from the signal. Goal 8 pursues the control and modification of the weather against extreme wind and rain, with named work streams in typhoon control, heavy-rainfall control, and the artificial generation of rain over the ocean to spare the land, and with a social-coupling model that governs when and where the intervention fires. The framing is public safety; the commitment is to actuate the atmosphere. The programs are set top-down, funded, dated, and assigned to named directors at Osaka University and the RIKEN research institute. The intent to build the components of this architecture is written into the goal statements, which is what makes the pattern legible on the public record rather than in inference.

7.4

The arteries

The program board names the state intent. A second layer carries that intent across the gap between a funded program and a product a person consents to, and the record of that layer is the capital. One institution is its spine. In-Q-TelThe Central Intelligence Agency's venture arm: stakes in Palantir, AndurilAutonomous sensing-and-effector company: Lattice, EagleEye, and the IVAS headset program., and Synchron., the venture arm the Central Intelligence Agency founded in 1999 to place intelligence-community money into commercial technology, seeded PalantirData-fusion company: Foundry, Gotham, and the MavenPalantir's Maven Smart System, a DoD-designated key system, contract ceiling past $1B. Smart System. with roughly two million dollars around 2005, when the agency was the company's only customer, and backed Anduril early. It holds positions across the geospatial and remote-sensing companies of the orbital tier, and its interest reaches the body: a 2016 investment, disclosed through a leak, placed it in a startup extracting DNA from the outer layer of the skin, and its November 2025 stake in SynchronEndovascular brain-computer interface, the Stentrode, backed by In-Q-Tel. placed it in the commercial brain-computer interface. The fund is the connective tissue between the state intent this part documents and the commercial layer where that intent becomes product.

Around that spine sit the model's private and sovereign copies. ARPA-HThe health-DARPA (2022), roughly $1.5B, a molecular-to-societal mandate., the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health established in 2022 and funded at roughly one and a half billion dollars, was modeled on DARPAUS Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the defense research arm behind the neural-interface lineage. and given a mandate its own charter describes as spanning the molecular to the societal, the medical-channel funding vehicle the dual-use bridge of Part Two predicts. Wellcome Leap, founded in 2020 by the Wellcome Trust and described in its own words as the first global version of DARPA, applies the model to the human body from private philanthropy and orchestrates a network of more than a million scientists and engineers. Open Philanthropy funds the emerging-technology policy layer, supplying the bulk of the more than fifty-seven million dollars that built the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown, the think tank where the doctrine of governed convergence is written and staffed. Britain's ARIA, documented in Part Six, is the sovereign instance of the same template, gathering the convergence under one exempt agency. The arteries run from the intelligence agency's own fund, through the health-DARPA and the private-DARPA, into the policy institute, and they carry money in one direction, from the state's intent toward the fielded product.

7.5

The rotation and the fielded product

The capital travels with people, and the people are a pattern in their own right. The same figures direct the defense agency, the platform company, the think tank, and the private moonshot fund, in sequence, carrying the design between them. Regina Dugan directed DARPA from 2009 to 2012, left to lead Google's advanced-technology group, moved in 2016 to run Facebook's Building 8, the division that pursued a type-by-brain non-invasive neural interface and the wrist-worn neural input that reached consumer hardware, and became chief executive of Wellcome Leap in 2020 to build, in her own framing, a DARPA for human health. Jason Matheny directed IARPAThe intelligence community's research arm: BRIAR, SMART ePANTS, MIST., the program board of Section 7.1, then served as Assistant Director of National Intelligence, founded the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown, took three White House technology-and-security posts in 2021, and became president of the RAND Corporation in 2022, the institution that published the 2020 report defining the Internet of Bodies. Renee Wegrzyn managed programs in DARPA's Biological Technologies Office, the same office that issued the N3DARPA Next-Generation Nonsurgical Neurotechnology, a read-write neural interface at ~16 mm³, no surgery. solicitation, left for the synthetic-biology company Ginkgo Bioworks and its biosurveillance arm, and returned in October 2022 as the founding director of ARPA-H. The doctrine theorist and the intelligence-policy architect share an address: Giordano holds his chair at Georgetown, and Matheny founded his think tank there, a documented affiliation carried with its interpretive weight marked.

The rotation ends at the fielded product, where the state's programs acquire commercial form. Several companies carry the pattern, each an operating software layer sold to the government, each the commercial instance of a capability documented elsewhere in this volume.

Palantir supplies the decision layer. Its Foundry platform binds an organization's data and logic into one operational model through what the company calls an ontology, and its Gotham platform, which the company names the operating system for defense decision making, fuses sensor and intelligence feeds into a targeting and decision layer, the commercial counterpart to the IARPA programs of Section 7.1. The company's Maven Smart System, an outgrowth of the earlier Project Maven, was designated a key military system by the Department of Defense, and the Army's contract for it grew from a prototype award near four hundred and eighty million dollars through a modification to seven hundred and ninety-five million and, in May 2025, a ceiling raised past one billion, with a NATO agreement following in April 2025. Maven is the fielded reasoning layer that compresses fused sensor data into targeting decisions at machine speed. In-Q-Tel, the fund of Section 7.4, seeded the company in its earliest years.

Anduril supplies the autonomy and effector layer. Its Lattice software, the operating system beneath a family of systems it calls Connected Warfare, states its purpose as connecting sensors, shooters, and decision-makers so that forces can act at the edge in seconds, the same collapse of the boundary between reading and acting that this volume tracks at the neural and molecular scales, realized at the scale of the battlefield. Its EagleEye, revealed in October 2025, is a family of warfighter augments delivering, in the company's words, AI-enhanced digital vision, threat detection, and connectivity in combat, powered by Lattice; Anduril assumed the Army's twenty-two-billion-dollar mixed-reality headset program from Microsoft in a handover announced in February 2025 and partnered with Meta on the effort in May. In-Q-Tel backed Anduril as well. In December 2024 OpenAI, which builds the decision layer documented in Part Eleven, entered a strategic partnership with Anduril to apply its models to counter-drone defense.

Armada supplies the compute base at the edge. Its ruggedized mobile data centers, deployable in as little as sixty days against the years a fixed facility takes, carry graphics-processor compute and satellite-grade connectivity into remote and contested environments, so the decision layer runs where the sensing happens rather than only in the central campus of Part Thirteen. The company reports operation across more than a hundred countries and names defense situational awareness and mission autonomy among its sectors.

Clearview AIFacial recognition at a distance. assembled a facial-recognition database from scraped public images, the productized instance of biometric identification at a distance. The program board documents the intent, the arteries document the money, the rotation documents the hand that carries the design, and the commercial layer documents the product a person actually meets. Part Eight documents the doctrine that names what all of it is for.
